body: The UK uses white front plates and yellow back plates. Some may have a blue or green strip, but most do not.
The UK, along with Ireland and Malta, drives on the left side of the road.
Double yellow lines on the side of the road indicate a no-stopping zone. This feature is also found in Ireland.
Middle lines with long dashes and cat's eyes (reflectors) in the gaps are a good clue for the UK.
The most common UK bollard has a rounded shape with a red front reflector and a white back reflector. It features a black base and top with a white stripe in the middle.
The UK uses wooden poles, often with pole steps made of thin horizontal metal rods bolted to the side. Ireland shares this feature.
UK chevrons are black with white arrows, distinguishing them from Irish (black with yellow) and French (blue with white) chevrons.
The UK uses standard European triangular warning signs with a red border and white background. This helps distinguish it from Ireland, which uses unique diamond-shaped yellow signs.
UK directional signs are blue, green, or white and use letters like A or M for major roads. Unlike Irish signs, they are not typically bilingual.
The UK often uses white street signs with black text, positioned low to the ground on two small posts. Some may have different colors or feature a cul-de-sac icon or coats of arms.
UK yield signs say "GIVE WAY", while Irish signs say "YIELD".
Yellow warning stickers on UK utility poles often show a person being zapped by a lightning bolt, which is absent on Irish stickers.
This yellow traffic bollard is a common sight in the UK.
Instead of signs, UK pedestrian crossings often feature distinctive black and white striped poles with a yellow bulb on top. This is also common in Ireland.
Rural UK metal gates often have square corners, unlike the rounded corners common on gates in Ireland and Northern Ireland.
The British countryside is very green, with many hedgerows and low, rolling hills. This landscape is very similar to Ireland.
Terraced and semi-detached houses are extremely common in the UK, similar to Ireland and the Netherlands.
Red brick buildings are a common architectural style in many parts of the UK.
UK suburbs often feature near-identical semi-detached houses with well-manicured lawns and maze-like road layouts.
Many British buildings have chimneys with multiple round, brick-coloured chimney pots.
Black-and-white timber-framed buildings can be found in the UK, and are less common in Ireland.
The UK has Generation 4 'smallcam' coverage, identifiable by its low-mounted position and large circular blur.
Finding one of the four country flags (England, Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland) can pinpoint your location within the UK.
The first digit of a main A-road number indicates the region in Great Britain.
UK landline area codes can help with location, for example, 028 is for all of Northern Ireland and 020 is for London.
Bins in urban areas often have the city name on them, providing a direct location clue.
The Scottish Highlands have a semi-barren, very mountainous landscape. Much of the coverage is from early spring, giving the vegetation a brown and yellow look.
Scotland often features bulky, round red and white bollards with a reflector that wraps all the way around.
Diamond-shaped 'Passing Place' signs are unique to Scotland.
The Welsh language on bilingual signs is a key indicator for Wales. Look for frequent use of letters like W, Y, and the double LL.
The word 'Araf' (Slow) painted on the road is a unique and common Welsh language marking found only in Wales.
Scottish Gaelic appears on road signs in the Scottish Highlands, often in green or yellow text. It shares similarities with Irish and uses letter clusters like bh, dh, and mh.
Houses made of large blocks of sandstone or granite are common in Scotland. Granite is typical for Aberdeen, red sandstone for Glasgow, and yellow sandstone for Edinburgh.
Cornish palms are most common in the far southwest of the UK, along the coast and in Jersey.
Black stickers with yellow text can sometimes be found on lampposts in Northern Ireland.
The Isle of Man, located in the Irish Sea, has only Generation 2 coverage and counts as part of the UK.
Jersey, an island in the English Channel, has only Generation 2 coverage and counts as part of the UK.
Gibraltar is a British Overseas Territory at the southern tip of Spain and counts as part of the UK.
Bermuda is a British Overseas Territory in the North Atlantic Ocean.
The Falkland Islands are a British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic Ocean.
South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands are a British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic Ocean.
The Pitcairn Islands are a British Overseas Territory in the South Pacific Ocean.
The British Indian Ocean Territory is a British territory in the Indian Ocean with Generation 2 trekker coverage. It counts as part of the UK.
The Lake District is very hilly, with many exposed rocks and stone walls, resembling but rockier than the Scottish Highlands.
London street signs are distinctive, showing the street name in black with postcode and borough in red.
Some Generation 4 coverage in London was captured by a white electric vehicle with a distinct rear; similar cars appear in Dublin and Germany.
Birmingham's poles and signposts mostly have yellow tape or paint, with lampposts usually bearing yellow stickers.
‘Twenty’s Plenty’ speed signs with green borders are common in and around Glasgow.
